m Ships, that either carried them over into Pentapolis crossing the River Nilus, or rather going down the River into the Mediterranean, and so to any part of those North parts of Africa, and others by Ship through the Red Sea to Arabia Faelix, which is that Aethiopia, which is here meant, though 'tis possible, in those dayes the African Aethiopia might, as once it did, extend quite to the mouth of the Red Sea, on whose shore their Ancestors must needs first land out of Arabia, whence the Habessines, who are our present Aethiopians, do own their descent. So Messengers by Ships might carry the news to both the Aethiopian, Asian, and African, by the Red Sea.

n In much security they had hitherto lived, the most potent, and formidable Neighbour having been their Antient Allie, till the news of so mighty an Enemy at their very Doors.

o Apprehensions of Danger, that puzzles their Wisdom, weakens their Courage, makes them in perplexity, both sick, and astonished.

p Either like that, which, when their Host was drowned in the Red Sea, seiz'd all Egypt, or rather like this latter fear, which arose from the Mighty havock made by the Chaldaean.

q A storm like that certainly cometh against you.

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:10
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
r The numerous Families, and Tribes.

s To dwindle, and decrease.

t By the Army, Power, and Conduct of Nebuchadnezzar.

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:11
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
u Nebuchadnezzar.

x His own Subjects, not hired Souldiers.

chap. 28.5.

y This is the description of them. Hab. 1.7. a fierce, and cruel people, as Psal. 147.8, 9.

z By the hand of God using means for that end, as before noted, chap. 29. ver. 4.

a Readily, and with Resolution not to sheath them, till Egypt be filled with slain.

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:12
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Isa. 19.9

Heb. [illegible].

b Either by some extraordinary drought, or rather, by means of that mighty Lake, that, which drew so much water from Nilus, that all their Canals were ever after shallow, and the Lake, as the Oracle foretold, helpt their Enemy, and hurt their Friends: or the Chaldaeans might divert them, and so their Fortified Towns would want one great defence.

c God gave it, here he sells; the one is proper, the other a borrowed expression, indeed God seems to pay wages with it. chap. 29. ver. 19, 20. but hereby is intimated, that as Sellers deliver into the hand of the Buyer, so God would deliver Egypt into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar as surely, as if he had bought it, and we may conclude, the Chaldaean as a Buyer, will make the most of all he buyes.

d Not of just, and compassionate, but of injurious, and merciless men.

Heb. the f[illegible] ness thereof.

e Who leave nothing, they can carry away, eat up, or spoil.

f 'Tis the Decree, and Edict of Heaven, which can't be broken.

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:13
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Jer. 43.12. [illegible] 46.25. [illegible]ech. 13.2.

g God did it by the Babylonians; those proud, and impious Nations did triumph over the Gods of the conquered, and out of contempt of them, burnt them, or broke them, as is well known, so Sennacherib threatned, 2 Chr. 32.19. Isaiah. 37.19, 24. against the true God, as he did to Idol Gods.

h Dunghil Gods, as the words, fitter to be trod under foot, then to be deck't, and respected.

i These nothings, as the word imports, whoever destroyed the Image, destroyed the God, for 'twas nothing but an Image.

k Memphis now grand Cair, the chief City of the Country, the seat of their Kings first, of their Priests by consequence, and of all their several Gods too; But the Chaldeans destroyed the nest, and birds too.

l Either an Egyptian born, or, independent, or over all Egypt, or that shall have the Power, Wealth, or Honour like a former brave Egyptian King.

m Of consternation, and cowardise that should disable them for counsel, and action in their most urgent Affairs.

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:14
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
n See cap. 29. ver. 14. let. m.

o It may be literally understood that Zoan, Tanis, for that is its name, should be burnt down to Ashes; or Metaphorically of War, and civil Dissensions.

Or, Tanis.

p A very great and populous City, scituate on one of the mouths of Nilus, and on the Sea, Nahum. 3.8. Now Alexandria stands, where that did, but 'twas greater in sin than in people, and it was visited with very great, and dreadful judgments. Nahum. 3.8, 9, 10, 11. which see.

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:15
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
q See chap. 21. ver. 31. let. d.

Or, Pelusium.

r Either Sain, or more likely Pelusium, which was a Frontier, and secured the entrance of Egypt fromward the Desert of Sin, was the key of Egypt, and therefore alwaies well fortified, and strongly garrisoned, it was called Damiata.

s One of the principal munitions of Egypt; for 'twas a good, and large Haven, and was strengthned with all needful Fortifications.

[illegible] when I have [illegible] off.

u Or the Riches, and Tumultuous noise, which the multitudes thereof made.

x If we read, as the Margin, 'tis plain, God does threaten Pel[illegible]sium after No is cut off; if we retain our own Translation, we must think of another City of that name, which God threatens with Sin: Now this may be Thebae Egyptiacae, or this City may be Hamon No called Diospolis, the City of Iupiter, possibly it may be the same mentioned already, and the threat repeated to confirm it.

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:16
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
y See ver. 14. let. o. and chap. 20. ver. 47. l. u. x. and v. 8. let. y.

z Ver. 15. let. r.

a See ver. 9. let. o.

b See ver. 14. let. p. and ver. 15. let. x.

c Her Walls, and Towers, and Fortresses battered, torn, and broken through by the continued violence of Engines, and by the assaults of the Souldiers.

d See ver. 13. let. k.

e Being the chief City where King and Councels sate, whence Orders should be given, whither all intelligences were brought, all should be so bad abroad, that nothing, but fears, and distresses fill their Ears, Mouths, and Hearts, beside the wants, that would increase dayly on them.

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:17
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
f 'Tis probable these might be a select Army of valiant youths in one body, collected out of these two Cities, that resolved to break the Chaldaean Army, or fall in the Enterprise, or else that they did to the utmost, defend the Walls, and were put to the Sword when the City was taken by assault.

Or, Heliopolis.

g Bethshemesh, and Heliopolis an Idolatrous City, that Worshipt the Sun, and in which was a stately Temple built to the Sun; Its greatness was 150 Furlongs, 6 miles, and 3 quarters in compass, a very vain and sinful City, as its name Aven intimates.

Or, Bubastum.

h Bubastus, and sometime called Haephestus, no inconsiderable place, and, I believe not far from Aven, it should seem to be some convenient pass, as I conjecture.

i The Citizens, Cities put for Citizens.

k Some of the first, it may be the very first, which put Memphis, at report of it into a sick fit, with great pain; this being the first fruits of the sad coming harvest.

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:18
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
l A great, and goodly City of Egypt, Tachapanes, Tachpanes, Tahapanes, Tahpanes, Chanes, and Hanes, Isai. 30.4. are Name[illegible] given it, and this from a Queen of Egypt of that name in Solomon's time, 1 King. 11.19, 20. it stood not far from Sin or Pelusium, and by the Greeks a little softening the Name, call'd Daphne Pelusiaca. 'twas a Royal City, in it Pharaoh had a house, to it many Iews fled, when forbidden of the Lord by the Prophet Ieremy, chap. 44. 'twas one of the first Cities you come to out of the Desert of Sin, and was one of the keys of Egypt.

Or, darkness[illegible] the day. Or, restrained.

m A night shall come upon it, and such a night of sorrow, as shall grow darker, and darker, till the day, i. e. their day be darkness, or else word for word, Darkness shall be the day, and may bear this sense, shall be more welcome, more useful, more desired, then the day, whose light would discover their flight, which the night concealed.

n As into shivers.

o The Scepters; for there was one of Pharaoh's houses, and probably, some Scepter, and other Regal Ornaments; or the Bars, which kept Enemies out, and secured the Citizens, and Country, such was this Frontier Town, or, when by giving this strong place into Nebuchadnezzars hand, I shall break the Kingdom of Egypt, that it no more oppress with yokes, i. e. burthens

p The Beauty, and Goodliness, with which the strength of this City was set out in her Buildings, Towers, Forts.

q Shall be buried in her own ruines.

r Sorrow by the success of the Chaldaeans against her, compared often to a cloud.

s Either Metaphorically, i. e. the Towns, and Villages about her, or literally, her Children, her Daughters only mentioned, because her Sons were destroyed, and slain.

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:20
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
t Of Ieconiah's Captivity three Moneths, and two Days before Ier[illegible]salem was taken, Ier. 52.4.

u The fourth day of our April.

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:21
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
x I have often told thee, I would break, now I tell thee I have broken, partly by the victory of the Chaldaean over Pharaoh Necho, partly by the victory the Cyrenaeans got over Pharaoh Hophra, to raise the siege, from which attempt he fell with shame and loss, but more by Civil Wars.

y Hophra or Apries.

Jer. 46.1[illegible].

z And this wound is incurable, it shall never be bound up to be healed, his Arm shall never be strong and fit to encounter a potent Enemy, as once it was.

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:22
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
a In the former verse God had broken the arm, in this he will break the Arms of Pharaoh, he will shew, he is still against Pharaoh, and will break him more, and more.

b That part of his Kingdom which remains intire.

c That, which was shattered before, That part of his Kingdom in Syria, taken from him from Euphrates, to the River of Egypt, that once was a strong arm, but now broken, and useless to him: And Egypt, whatever strength it now hath, shall be as weak, and useless too, thus all his power, and strength shall be destroyed.

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:23
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: Vid. chap. 29. ver. 12. let. g. and chap. 20. ver. 23. let. o. where the same expressions are.

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:24
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
d Give the first strength, and continue it with new supplys, so that with strength from God, he shall proceed.

e His strength shall have a weapon suited, and proportion'd to it, and what will be hard, where God's Sword and his strength are engaged to effect it?

f Hophra.

g Not only, as the stoutest must, when nature breaks, but cry out, and sigh, or howl not becoming a brave man.

h King of Babylon.

i Who hath given him his deadly wound, under which he roars, while he hath any strength, and groans, when his voice sails him. It speaks sore griefs, and deep sense of them; as Exod. 2.24. Iudg. 2.18. Iob 24.12.

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:25
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: These two forgoing verses are a repetition of God's threats against Pharaoh, and of his promises to assist Nebuchadnezzar in the War, and every thing plain in them.

entries.title: Ezekiel 30:26
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: Vide ver. 23.

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:1
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
a As chap. 30. ver. 20. let. t.

b Our Iune 26th day old stile, the 16th day new stile;Calvisi[illegible]s. Vsserius. just one moneth, and eight dayes be[illegible]fore the taking of the City on the 27th of Iuly, vet. stil. but 17th of Iuly, new stile.

c Tam[illegible]z.

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:2
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
d Apries, or Hophra.

e His numerous Subjects, with the power, and Riches they Glory in.

ver. 18.

f Bethink thy self, what King of all before thee, art thou equal with, or else greater? On what surer, and more immoveable Foundation doth thy greatness stand? That thou dreamest of a perpetual quiet, and flourishing state in the midst of all thy sins, and wickednesses?

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:3
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
g Kingdom, and its Kings were the greatest, the world ere knew before thee, they had longest time of growth through 1340, or 1360 years from Belus, who was Nimrod, or Belus Assyrius, to Sardanapalus, from 1719, or 1717, or 1718 to 3059. of the World. And they had as fair advantages, as reaching a foresight, and as unwearied diligence to advance the Kingdom; yet I brought it down.

h Like a Cedar; Kings and Kingdoms oft compared to Trees, both in profane, and sacred Emblems, or like the most Goodly Cedar for Strength and Beauty.

i A great Mountainous tract from East to West, 125 mile in length, encloseth Canaan on the North.

Heb. fair of branches.

k Which are the Beauty, Greatness, Strength of the Tree, so had this mighty Kingdom fair Provinces, as Branches springing from it.

l What we render shadowing in the Hebr. may signifie, either silent, and quiet, or framing, and modelling, intimating, that this Kingdom, like a shady Tree, gave shelter to the weak, as if fram'd artificially to this, and 'twas a silent, quiet repose its Subjects had; as weak Creatures find shelter in a mighty wood, so these.

m This Kingdom grew to great height, while its branches were so beneficial.

n Or Clouds, for so the word will without violence bear; Cloud being called so from their thickness; however, the Head among the thick boughs speaks the magnificence, and greatness of this King compassed about with Tributary Kings, and Princes, and Mighty men.

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:4
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
o As Cedars grow great by the water courses, so this Kingdom by multitudes of people, convenience of Trade, by the plenty of the Country, if no Trade, for 'twas first planted in the fruitful fields among the sweet Rivers, Euphrates, Tigris, Lycus, Diava, and others.

Or, nourished.

p The Sea sent out her Waters, which gave being to the Rivers, that water'd him, and improved him; whereas Egypt, thy Rivers arise out of a Lake, which, though great, not to be compared with the deep.

Or, brought him [illegible]p.

q The Provinces of this mighty Kingdom, that are like plants about a great Tree.

Or, conduits.

r Beneficence, Justice, Protection, encouragements, that Subjects need, and good Princes disperse among them, so the deep filled this King, and he sent out his streams.

s To all his Subjects in his Kingdom.

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:5
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
f His Power, Glory, and his Pride too, run up on high, a just administration of Laws for benefit of the publick, and a kind usage of the Subject, while 'twas here, made the King great, and his Kingdom famous.

u Above all his Neighbour Kings, among whom oppressed weaklings still came to this Kingdom, while just, for shelter.

x Many became his Subjects by voluntary choice, and his Native Subjects increast in numbers, and Wealth.

y The Provinces reacht far and wide by the conquest of his armes, or attractives of his kindness brought to unite with him.

z The many streams of Royal Justice and Beneficence sent forth from the Throne of this Kingdom, so his Throne was advanced and established.

Or, [illegible] sent them [illegible]

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:6
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Dan. 4.[illegible]

a Not every individual, but all sorts, and kinds of Men and People, Nobles, Merchants, Husbandmen likened to Fowles.

b Did settle their Habitations, and Families, expecting what they found, safety, and rest, and hoping, what did ensue, an increase of their Children and Posterity as Birds do in a quiet, and safe nest.

c In his Kingdom, in the Cities, or Towns of it.

d The very same thing exprest by a new Hieroglyphick: Beasts here are people, the Field is the Countreys round about, their bringing forth their young includes their making their Dens, that is mens building, begetting children, and breeding them under his branches, under his Government, and Protection.

e This gives some light to the riddle. No Nation, that was great at that time in the World, but, either own'd the Dominion, or sought the Alliance, and Friendship of this King and Kingdom.

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:7
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
f Beautiful, lovely, and desirable.

g Not exerted in Tyranny, and oppression, but exercised in the Royal Art of imitating the greatest, and best Being, who is King over all, for he doth good to all.

h How far soever remote, yet the Justice, and Goodness of the Government appeared, the Beauty of those Provinces as well as of the whole Kingdom.

i Whence he sprang, which supported, and supplyed the Kingdom, was Right, the Laws, Punishments, rewards, and encouragements, neither founded in cruelty, nor maintained by violence.

k Not by blood, which is no proper kindly nourishment for such Cedars, but by Waters, which are kindly, and proper, and these great enough for his own growth, and to nourish others too.

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:8
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
l Kings, the greatest, and most magnificent.

Gen. 2.[illegible]

m Either in the most fruitful Gardens, or in Iudah and Israel not David, not Solomon, Iehoshaphat, or Hezekiah could top, and shade him.

o A meaner sort of Trees, emblem of lesser Kings, and Kingdoms, these were but like his boughs, though they grow to great height, and bulk.

p The same in another allusion, Kings like Chesnut trees, great, when by themselves, yet compared with this Assyrian, were but as branches of his boughs, all which in Isaiah's words, cap. 10.7, 8. there was some truth, though more pride in this Speech of the Assyrian, which the Prophet reports.

q All summed up, none like him in all the Kingdoms of the World.

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:9
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
r All this greatness, Wealth, and Glory I have given him.

s The numbers of his Provinces, and multitude of his Subjects, high, and low, great, and small.

t Either did when they saw his greatness, or would have envied, if they had seen it, or, if there may be a seeming justifiableness in wondring at anothers Glory, and wishing it our own, here it might be found.

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:10
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
n Now you shall hear the sin, and the fall of this great Kingdom of Assyria.

o His mind could not longer bear so great prosperity, he lifts up himself, and in his pride forgets God, who lifted him up, and will cast him down, you have a Specimen of it in that of Isa. 10.7, 8, 9. with the rest to the 20th. verse, and Isa. 36.9.15, 18. this, as other best framed polities degenerated into pride, and violence against Neighbours, Subjects, Friends as well as against Enemies, though too much 'twas, to despise man, yet 'twas intolerably more insolent, to reproach God. It is but time to lop, nay cut down this Cedar, as Isa. 10.33. with Isa. 37.36, 38.

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:11
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
p No Prophetick stile, as some think, I have, because I will, for most certainly God would deliver.

q Proud King of Assyria, who inherited all the vices of his Progenitors more, than their Kingdoms, infamous Sardanapalus.

r Some say Cyrus, rather Arbaces, who first strook at the root of this Cedar, and cut him down, and well might this man, though no King when he attempted this, be stiled the mighty one of the Heathen, who could bring together four hundred thousand of Medes, Pe[illegible]sians, Babylonians, and Arabians a power sufficient to besiege the Assyrian King two years in his own City, and Palace.

Heb. in doing [illegible]hall do unto [illegible].

s So he did, for he held him besieged without hope of relief, till at two years end, this vicious King burnt himself with his Palace.

t With disgrace, for his lewd shameless courses, as a Wife is cast out by divorce for Adultery, Lev. 21.7.

u So Sardanapal[illegible]s was cast out for his effeminacy, and lewdness; for 'tis reported, this gave Arbaces first encouragement to lay a des[illegible]gn against him, who was driven out, as the Prophet words it, by the breach of two mile and half wideness, made by the mighty floods from continual Rains, which the walls of Nineve could not withstand, so God rather then man did drive this beast out.

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:12
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
c Forreigners, who regard neither justice, nor mercy, such were those, which made up this Army of Arbaces the Mede.

chap. 28.7.

d So these were for their strength, and valour much, but for their numbers, and barbarity, more to be dreaded.

e Not shall, for 'twas down before Ezekiels time, about the time Ezekiah was born, and about 240 years before the destruction of Ierusalem, and the Babylonish Captivity.

f Revolted or forsaken Sardanapalus.

g As a Tree, that growing on the Mountains, which hang over the Valleys, when it falls, breaks, and its branches are scattered in the lower ground, on the banks of Rivers, that run in the bottom, so is this mighty Cedar, this King, and Kingdom fallen from highest power, and honour into deepest contempt and impotence, not able to repell his Adversaries, or escape out of their hands.

h All, that were Tributary to him, have withdrawn their Tribute, and rejected his Dominion, and such as were his Allies, and depended on his Patronage, have quit their Leagues, and dependences, and left his shadow.

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:13
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
i His broken state.

k Which built, and bred there, shall now despise the Tree, and triumph over it.

l The same in another emblem, as ver. 6. Beasts, Fowls, People, and Nations, that were sheltred under the shadow of this Tree, shall all, as is the custom of all, of them, get from under it, and with the first insult and trample upon the body, boughs, and branches, Fowles get on it and both pick and defile, Beasts rustle through it and brouse on the broken branches.

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:14
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
m All this is designed to be a warning to mortals.

n i. e. the Emperours, Potentates, Kings, or rich flourishing States.

o Planted most commodiously, and furnisht most abundantly with Power, and Wealth.

p Grow proud, because they are high, shoot out tops above all the t[illegible]ick boughs their Neighbours. This caution against pride, and self exalting is three times repeated, that all, especially great men, and this proud King of Egypt, to whom this Parable is propounded, should be humble.

Or, stand upon [illegible]selves for [illegible]heir height.

q For if by office they are Gods, yet by nature, they are men, and by the decree of God, who cannot die, these Gods must, as men, dye, be laid in the grave, forgotten like other men, like the Children of mean men, for that death, and the grave make no distinction. Be not proud, God will pull down such, be humble, you must dye.

Psal. 82.7.

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:15
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
r The King of Assyria, the tall Cedar, or the Kingdom of Assyria,

s Was a man in grave; buried in its own ruins.

t There was much lamentation.

u I put the Sea, i. e. Either neighbouring States, or the body of his people, or the trading part of the World, into mourning for him.

o All publick affairs; Commerce, and Friendly intelligences, were at a great stand.

p The great traffick and wealth by it, which did flow, as great waters, were staid, and living Rivers were, as void of motion, as the dead Sea, all was out of course.

q The field, in which this Cedar grew, i. e. the whole Kingdom of Assyria.

Heb. be [illegible].

s Fell into a swound at the News of this great, and unparallel'd downfal of this mighty King, and Kingdom, which hath been here in sacred Hyperbole set forth to warn Egypt, and convince it, none can stand whom God will cast down. Whether there were any portentous signs in the Sea, and great Waters, and the Rivers, and among the trees, presages of this fall, and pointed at here, I enquire not.

r All the lesser Kings, and Princes about him

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:16
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
t All that heard the noise of his fall trembled at it, 'twas, as God intended it should be, an astonishment to them all.

u Brought the King, and Kingdom, as a dead man to the grave among them, that before were dead, and buried.

x All Kings, and particularly the greatest, and richest called here the choice, and best of Lebanon.

y Did enjoy great Power, Riches, and worldly Glory.

z 'Tis a Prosopopaeia, and he speaks of the dead with allusion to the manner of the living, who rejoice to see the proud brought, as low as the lowest, thus the Prophet, Isa. 14.9, 10.

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:17
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
a Either his neighbour Kings and Princes, or those that were his own Subjects, but rich and mighty.

b Were broken and perisht with him, and went to those God had slain for their pride and wickedness.

c His loyal and faithful Subjects and Friends abroad, who having been protected by him, remembred it, and adhered to him to support him; but all fell, are extinct, and gone down to the pit, where many proud, but no pride; where all know themselves dust and ashes, and God glorious, holy and just.

entries.title: Ezekiel 31:18
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
verse 2.

d The mightiest, richest, and longest lived Kingdom I have represented, saith God, overthrown, and destroyed; a Kingdom thou canst not pretend to equal, and if not like this, what King or Kingdom art thou like, that thou shouldst be invincible?

e Who ere thou art like in height, and power thou shalt be like them in thy s[illegible]ll, and ruine.

f As unclean, despised, and loathsome in thy blood, like the slain with the Sword, not to be known, without an upbraiding inscription: This is Pharaoh.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:1
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
a Of the Captivity of Ieconiah.

b Answering to part of our February, and part of March, and called S[illegible]bat.

c And was the 15th of Febr. vet. stil. and the 5th new stile.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:2
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
d See chap. 19. ver. 1. let. a. b. c. and [illegible]hap. 27. ver. 2. let. a. b.

e Hop[illegible]ra.

f This Hieroglyphick see chap. 19. ver. 3. let. s. and ver 6. let. i.

g Among, or to the Nations round about thee, spoiling all thou canst, a cruel devourer abroad.

Or, Dragor.

h A Crocodile, a devouring Dragon in thy Rivers at home, for there the Crocodiles lay, and did m[illegible]schief, though sometimes they went down the River to the Sea.

i That comes forth to seek prey, and devour, so a Lion at Land, a Whale, or Crocodile rather, at S[illegible], ravenous every where.

k Raisedst mighty A[illegible]mies, and didst lead them out ag[illegible]inst thy Neighbours, as in particular, cap. 29.3, 4.

l The People, Kingdoms, and Kings near thee.

m With thy Souldiers.

n Disturbedst, and mudd[illegible]edst their pleasant clearness, and madest them unfit to drink, i. e, Didst spoil all the pleasant and useful conveniencies of thy Neighbours.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:3
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
chap. 12.13. and 17.20.

o A large, long, and wide net, drawn out to full extent.

p With which both Lions, and Crocodiles might be taken, and in which this Lion and Crocodile should certainly be taken; for God, whose hand never erreth, will spread the net.

q In the Countreys, where these Creatures were hunted; for they went in mighty companies to the Game, as they accounted it.

r Drag thee along to destroy thee, pull thee up out of the Pit, in which the Net was laid to take the Lion to kill him and draw this Crocodile up out of the water for the same end; In brief, War by land, and Sea by a confederacy of many people against Hopbra shall be Gods ner, wherein he shall be taken, kept a Prisoner, as he was, and at last strangled, see chap. 29. ver. 4. let. t.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:4
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
s Thy beaten Army shall be slain, see chap. 29.5. ver. it was literally fulfilled in the Deserts of Lybia, where the slain of Hophr[illegible]'s Army were left to be devoured by Fowles, and Beasts. Metaphorically 'tis gathering a mixture of people, Souldiers, like ravenous Birds and Beasts from all parts to spoil Egypt.

u They should not be removed, till filled with the spoils of Egypt.

x The Forreign, and mercenary Souldiers shall be enricht by the slaughter, and plunder of the Egyptians.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:5
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
y Throw, or cast.

z The Carcasses of thy slain men, and Souldiers.

a Whither they retired for safety.

b Not so fill them, as to equal them in height with Hills, but we say a man fills a place, who scatters much, or many things, though but on the surface, so here Va[illegible]leys filled.

c With the Carcasses of thy Princes, as the Chald. Paraphrast I think hits right: And so the French (Et remplirai les valle[illegible]s de tes Glorieux qu'on aura abbatus.)

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:6
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
d Most plentifully pour out thy blood, as water is poured out to water Land, when men float their grounds.

Or, the land of thy swimming.

e Either because of the plenty thereof, wherein they swim'd, as we speak, or else because this King was a Whale, or Crocodile, his dwelling must be the Waters, and in them he swimmeth.

f An Hyperbole, blood shall be poured sorth, as if it were to rise to the very mountains, and cover them, or thy blood shall be shed through all thy plain Countrey, to the very Mountains, which I think are toward the South-west parts toward Aethiopia; so they should be slain from Migdol or Magdala to Syene, as chap. 29.10.

g Of thy Blood, and of thy Carcasses cast into the Rivers by thine Enemies, or drown'd in attempting flight by water from the drawn sword.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:7
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Or, extinguish.

h As a Torch is extinguisht, Isa. 43.17. so I will put out thy light, and turn thee into darkness.

Isa. 13.10. Joel 2.31. and 3.15. Mat. 24.29.

i Either by dark Vapours that arise from Blood, and putrifying Carcasses, which darken the Heavens, or 'tis a Description of great sorrows, fears, troubles, and perplexities; or else it may intimate particularly the total ruine of the whole Kingdom, in which the best, greatest, and noblest parts are, as Heaven, suppose the Government, the Sun, the King, the Moon, the Queen, the Stars, the Princes, and Nobles, Bright Lights, the most eminent of the Subjects for Wisdom, and Understanding, and then the Land, the Common People. All shall be covered with Clouds, and darkness of misery first, and sorrow next; or 'tis possible, that some unusual darknesses might be seen in the Heavens, and on the Earth about that time.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:8
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Heb. [illegible] the light in [illegible].

Heb. [illegible] dark.

These two foregoing verses contain the same thing four times with a little variation, repeated to affect the hearer, and to impress it the more deeply on their minds.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:9
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Heb. [illegible] to [illegible] gri[illegible]f.

k It speaks a passion mixt, and made up with grief for what is done, fear of the consequence of it, Anger against him, that did it, and an astonishment at the report, and it seiseth the heart, and spirits of the hearers.

l And great Nations.

m Either the same of it, or the remainders that fled timely from thy destruction, or thy Captives, who after thou art destroyed, are carryed away, and the news of thy fall with them, or when the like ruin and destruction shall fall upon them.

n Such as were strangers to Egypt, and which Egypt had no Commerce with, shall be troubled with apprehension what mischief may come upon the World from so mighty a Conqueror, and by the accession of so great a Kingdom, and Power, as that of Egypt.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:10
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
o And mighty people too.

p Astonisht and puzzel'd not knowing what resolutions to take, what advices to follow, or what to do.

q Who usually are, and in reason should be undaunted, and discovers no signs of fear, shall discover mighty disorders of fear and doubt, both for Egypt, and themselves.

r Vid. chap. 27. ver. 35. let, e. f.

s Or make my sword pass with such speed, as if it did fly along their borders, or hover near them, and so threaten them.

chap. [illegible]

t Be greatly afraid, lest Nebuchadnezzar, who here is Gods Sword, should smite them.

u Every one of the Kings, whose Kingdoms are near to Egypt, and by whose Borders the Babylonish Army must pass in their marches.

x They should be solicitous, not for the outmost parts of their Kingdoms, or for their Subjects, but for their own life.

y When they shall hear of Hophra beaten, taken, imprisoned, his Kingdom taken from him, and he dead by a shameful death, and all his people slain, captivated, spoiled, or fled.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:11
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
z See chap. 30.24, 25.

a Both King, and Kingdom of Egypt.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:12
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
b The Souldiers of Nebuchadnezzar helpt also by Amasis, and the rebellious Egyptians, that joined with Amasis and Nebuchadnezzar against their own King.

c The people of the Land, which were numerous before they were wasted by these Wars.

chap. [illegible].[illegible]

d See chap. 31. ver. 12. let. d.

e Break her Strength, rob her Treasures, sack her Cities, captivate her People, and make the Kingdom Tributary, and so stain all her Glory.

f From high to low, the great, and the mean promiscuously shall perish.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:13
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
g The Sheep, and Oxen devoured by hungry Chaldaean Souldiers, or else driven away: The Horses taken up to mount the Horsemen of the Chaldee Army, whose own Horses were tired, or spoiled.

h The Pastures lying along the Rivers side, and along their Canals, should be emptied of all Cattel, with which once they were full.

chap. 2[illegible].[illegible]

i There should be so few men left in Egypt, that they should not, as formerly, disturb the waters by digging, swimming, or rowing on them, or else, no more trouble the waters with the passing of mighty Armies over them to invade their Neighbours.

k So few Horse or Cows, that they should not at watering times, or in heat of the day soul the waters by running into them, and stamping, or trampling in them: but the Waters shall continue pure, and undisturb'd.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:14
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
l The sense literally this, the Waters undisturbed shall be clear, the mud settled at the bottom, and the waters above it of good depth,

m Smooth, and softly, as oyl, glides along, which will be when, neither Men, nor Cattel d[illegible]sturb the Rivers: but figuratively waters, and Rivers are People, and Nations, and those near to and once disturbed, and put into confusion by Egypt, at whose fall all those troubles shall cease, the people shall settle in quiet State, and Affairs shall, like a quieted River, run smoothly, and in great peace.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:15
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
n The former verse assures us of what it foretold and the assurance is the Word, and Truth of God; this ver[illegible]e tells us, when this shall be.

Heb. desolate [illegible] the fulness [illegible]ereof.

o This phrase is chap. 12.19. let. y.

p Men; and Women, Cattle, Food, Wealth, and Peace.

q By the Sword, the destroying Sword of the Chaldaeans.

r Then shall they confess it to the Glory of God's Power, and Justice.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:16
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
s This heavy, mournful, and sad account, which the Prophet hath given of the State of Egypt.

t The Funeral Speech of this Kingdom, for this, as Funeral Orations, tell us what was their Antient Glory, and what is now their miserable reproach and loss.

u Her Friends, or the Egyptians themselves rather.

x This may be expository of the former, and tell us who they are, that shall lament Egypt. The Provinces, and Cities of their Neighbouring Nations, or literally, the Daughters, the tender hearted Virgins, and Women abroad.

y Ruin'd Egypt.

z The common people, many of which suffered for what they could not prevent, a sort of people, that were fitter to be pitied, and spared, then to be rob'd, and slain, a sort of people, none but unrelenting hearts could be harsh to, or hasty with.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:17
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
a See ver. 1. let. a. b.

b About the [illegible]9th of February New Stile, or the 1st. of March, Old Stile.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:18
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
c Prepare the Funeral Ceremonies at the burial of Egypt, compose a suitable Song or Speech, utter it with a like suitableness to the sad occasion. Ier. 9.17, 18, 19. and Amos 5.16. use the word, and the places read will explain this.

d Either declare, that they shall be cast down from their height, and glory, or because this was done already, rather lay them down as dead in the Grave, bring him to his Grave, as the word is used with addition of Sheol. 1 King. 2.9. and much like are chap.. 26.20. let. b. d. and chap. 31.16. let. u.

e And celebrate the Funerals of other Cities, and Kingdoms, that lie buried in their own ruines, and other mens oblivion.

d A well known description of the state of the Dead, and the Grave.

e Usually this is no more, than a common Description of mens going to the dust in their Burial, but here it includes more. The Egyptians affected to be buried, either in the Isle Chemnis, or in the Pyramids, their Kings, and great ones thus would be laid by themselves, but Ezekiel provides them their grave among common people, burys them, where they fall; for they shall not have what they account so much of in their Funeral.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:19
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
f The Prophet begins with this question Dialogue-wise, Art thou better than others, that thou shouldest not die, and be laid in dust, as well as all others; speak Hophra, if thou hast any priviledge to plead, what hast thou to say, why thou shouldest not go down to the Pit, as a despised mortal?

g The Prophet hearing no plea of Priviledge adjudgeth him to the Grave, or lays him down with somewhat a sarcasm, go down like others.

h Take up thy Lodging, thy long, dark, and dismal recess where thy dust and bones shall never be known by any Royal Figure.

i Among prophane and loathed Carcasses, such the uncircumcised were in the opinion of the circumcised, and Herodotus in Euterpe saith, the Egyptians were circumcised. However in Scriptures, a Burial with the uncircumcised is a note of dishonour, and contempt; thus for the King and Princes.

The whole, from this verse, is a most Elegant personating of the Dead, as if sensible, and acquainted, and discoursing with, and rejoycing at the fall of proud Tyrants, who took not warning by their [illegible]all. Such a Prosspopaeia you have Isa. 14. In this Chapter, the Actors, are the Prophet, the King of Egypt, and his people, and their Auxiliaries.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:20
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
k The Egyptians.

l In Battle shall die.

m Of either one another in civil War, or of their Neighbours, they invaded, or of Babylonians, that invaded them.

Or, the sword is said.

n The whole Egyptian Kingdom is given up of God.

o Of wasting Enemies, especially of the Chaldaean.

p Make no Ceremony more than usually is made, when common Souldiers slain in the Field, where the Battle is fought, are drag'd by scores into mighty pits, and thrown into them promiscuously; or, as the enterlude will bear it, suppose any of them unwilling to stoop, draw them to it against their will.

q Of Souldiers, and People, Subjects, Allies, and helpers of Egypt.

Now the Prophet determines concerning the people, which die as others, fall undistinguisht, and, as such undistinguisht, must be laid in the pit.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:21
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
r The powerful, the valiant, whose natural strength of Body was great, and their courage greater, those that were strongest.

s For Feats, they did, by which it appeared they might, compared with others, pass for Giants, Mighty Warriours, Conquerors, and Rulers.

t The King of Egypt.

u Or, rather the Grave, where they lie without strength, as dead Mortals, tho' while they lived, they bore themselves, as if Gods, and immortal.

x Either these great ones shall speak to Hophra's helpers, or else these his friends slain in his quarrel, and dead before him, shall speak to him.

y To the Grave, See ver. 18. let. d.

z Neglected, and forgotten, or remembred with contempt, see ver. 19. let. i.

The Prophet seems in this verse to introduce the next speakers in this Parlee, and bringing them in, gives their character.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:22
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
a The famous, warlike, victorious Kings of Assyria.

b In the state of the dead, in the Land of Darkness, and Oblivion.

c Princes, Captains, Souldiers, Subjects, and Confederates.

d Perhaps his the greater, yet a Grave, and they about him, who were slain with him.

e Some in Wars, whilest the Kingdom began, grew, and flourisht, others, when the Kingdom was destroyed, these fell by the sword, a while their sword was longest, at last a longer sword, that of Arbaces the Mede, with his complices wounds Ashur to the heart, and he is brought to the Grave.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:23
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
f At least for Decorum here is supposed a spacious Vault, or Pit, in midst whereof the King of Ahur in a stately Tomb lies buried, and round about the Vault places to lay others dead with him, and in his cause, some of his more famous Captains, and Commanders.

g The common Subjects, and Souldiers of the Assyrian Empire, all buried undistinguisht about her, see ver. 22. let. d.

h The ruins of an Empire are its Grave, and so all the Subjects of this Empire lie buried with it.

Or, dismaying.

i Were a terrour to all they would be Enemies to; and proudly boasted of, and inhumanely used, their power now lie quiet, their dust little regarded, less feared, and least of all pitied.

k While they were in the Land of the living, a periphrasis of life.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:24
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
l The Persians, and their great, famous Kings, who lived in former days.

m Ver. 22. l[illegible]t. c. and [illegible]r. 23. l[illegible]t. g. h.

Vid. v[illegible]r. 22.

o See [illegible]er 20. l[illegible]t. [illegible].

p Vid. v[illegible]r. 20. l[illegible]t. z.

q Vid. ver. 1[illegible]. l[illegible]t. d.

r See v[illegible]r. 23. let. i.

s God, and Man poured contemp[illegible] upon them and punisht them for their pride, and turn[illegible]d t[illegible]eir Glory into shame whose vices, and miscarriages are more remembr[illegible]d, then their Noble Facts, and Glorious Atc[illegible]ievement[illegible].

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:25
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
t [illegible]ome co[illegible]c[illegible]ive t[illegible]e Prophet may allude to the manner of bur[illegible]ing [illegible]ith the [illegible], who had their Coffins, or Sepulchri[illegible] [illegible], in which with balms and spices the dead were kept, and these Ch[illegible]sts placed in midst of places provided for them; in such is the K[illegible]ng of [illegible] here placed with his slaughterd Captains a[illegible]out him, Vid. v[illegible]r. 23. let. h.

x ver. 22. let. c.

y [illegible]. [illegible]. l[illegible]t. d.

z ver. 24. let. s.

a See ver. 20. let. l.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:26
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
a See chap. 27. [illegible]. 13. let. l.

b Vid. c[illegible]ap. 27. ver. 13. let. k. to which interpre[illegible]tion I still adhere, adding that in the full extent of these Mos[illegible]hi, and [illegible], these Cappado[illegible]ians, and Albanians, the [illegible] may be in[illegible]luded, many of which were next Neighbours to them. [illegible] i[illegible] of opinion that the [illegible] are here meant, and so am I, but 'twill be said, they never had such a se[illegible]le[illegible] Kingdom worth noting. 'Tis true of that barbarous people no account, that ere they were Lords of the World yet they caused their terrour in the Land of the Living, were slain by the Sword under the Command and in the Expeditions of their Kings into Asi[illegible], who were accompanied with her multitudes. [illegible] reports they wasted Asia 3[illegible]0 years before Ro[illegible] was thought of, and that's about 1082 years before Christ's b[illegible]rth. Again we find them in armes, (no doubt in numbers much like what they appeared in, when To[illegible]ris their Queen destroyed C[illegible]rus, or when they have moved against their Neighbours in later dayes) and with those armes wasted the Cimmerii, a people seated near them on the Euxine Sea, and M[illegible]otis pal[illegible]s, and about that time they did under their Chief[illegible]ains waste Asia, they forced Cyaxares from the siege of Ni[illegible]eve[illegible] such consi[illegible]rable strength they were then of, this was 634 before Christ's birth, about 117 after Rome was built; about this time, or in this expedition, they took Sardis the Royal seat of Crae[illegible]us, Mag[illegible]is [illegible] sardibus [illegible]. ad A[illegible]n. m. 3340. to which Ovid gave the Title of Great, only the Castle held out. These Scythians in those days were a terrour to the Nations. Nay Hel[illegible]ious tells me from Herodotus, that they had the Imperial Power, were Lords of Asia for 28 years, and it seems, that their power was such, Cyaxares was glad to decline plain dealing, and to overthrow them by a wile, as Calvisius tells us ad Ann. M. 3344, and the help of Halyattes, King of the Lydians. These things were fresh in memory when Ezekiel prophesied thus against Egypt, for they fell out about the Eighth or Ninth year of Pharaoh Necho, some Fourteen years before Pharaoh Hophra came to the Crown; now about the Sixth year of his Reign, came this word of the Lord to Ezekiel; so that the Prophet might well mention these, as instances of Gods power abating the pride, and destroying the Kingdome of the Mighty, and these are with reason brought in among the Persians, and Assyrians.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:27
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
c The leaders of these Scythians were not buried with a pomp like that of Ashur, or Elam, but surprised by the fraud of Halyattes and Cyaxares, were cut off with all their multitude, and tumbled into pits with the rabble.

Heb weapons of their war.

d A Ceremony observed in pompous Funerals of great Captains, to have their Weapons, and their Armour carryed before the Hearse.

e Either, when carryed out to be buryed, or laid under their Head in their Graves; or perhaps under the Statues of them made, and laid on the tops of their Tombs; these Barbarous Scythians were not so buried.

f The exemplary punishment of their iniquity.

g Shall be seen upon their bones unburied, and cast out on the Earth by the just judgment of God.

h Because they were cruel,pour ce que bloody, ravenous, and mischievously Tyrannical, while they lived.

i Cyaxares, and the Persians, that durst not again attempt Nineve, till the Scythians were fallen.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:28
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
k Chief of Mesech, and Tubal, though not named.

l Shall be killed with the rest of wicked followers.

m Without regard, hurled into the pit with the common Souldiers, as thou fallest with them,

n Whose Throats were cut after they were taken.

o Of Halyattes and his Lidyans, in revenge 'tis like of the spoil done to Sardis, and by Cyaxares, in revenge of the affront they gave him, forcing him to quit the siege of Nineve, and by giving him Childs flesh to eat, pretending it was Venison taken by them in hunting.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:29
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
p The Posterity of Esau, the name of the Country too, in which they dwelt.

q Which had been many, and some great Warriours,

r Or Dukes, as Gen. 36.20, 21.

s Shew'd in the Assistance, they gave the Assyrians.

Heb. [illegible] or pa[illegible].

t Are slain, and laid aside to be buried, as Commanders are usually after their Death regarded, and their Bodies kept for a Funeral.

u Yet as the uncircumcised, so these must to the Pit, though no mention made of their being a terrour to the Nations.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:30
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
x Of all those Countreys, Tyrians, Zidonians, Assyrians, and Syrians, &c. which lay Northward from Iudea, now swallowed up by the Babylonian.

y Conquer'd, and slain.

z Their terrour is buried with them.

a When it appeared a vain confidence, and too weak to resist the Enemy, and save themselves.

b Scorned, and cast out, as profane, and loathsome.

c Of their conquering Enemy.

d They lie under a shameful fall, from a seeming Glory, to a Real Ignominy.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:31
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
e Hophra shall go to them by a like destruction, and, as if he did see them all ruined, as he was, shou'd

f Be comforted, or rejoyce, others before him met with the same fatal end, and, what ere comfort this might be, 'tis all he shall ever have, did he know all those things, and persons, that are here represented, and personated to us.

entries.title: Ezekiel 32:32
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
g It is God that speaketh, who had punisht former Tyrants, and by a retaliation, that the World might see his just Judgments: They were a terrour to the world by their cruelty, oppression, and continued violence, by their Covetousness, Ambition, and Pride; And God hath made them a terrour by his just severities in their punishments; And so, saith God, will I do with Pharaoh;

h That is, Pharaoh Hophra.

i Shall suffer, as they, since he sinned, as they, he made himself like them by choice of their vices, and I will make him like them by like miseries, and just recompences, and these shall be to his Subjects, as well as to himself. To Hophra, who was strangled, and likely cast out without Burial: To Amasis, who was taken out of his Tomb, and burnt to Ashes; so unlike the condition of the dead, which usually is rest to the body, was their condition after Death, who in life made it unlike, and imagined it was above the condition of Mortal men.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:2
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
a The Prophet, after three years silence injoined him, now hath his mouth opened by new Commission.

b To the Iews in General, to whom he had not spoke since what he spake in the 24th Chapter.

c Propound a parable unto them.

Heb. [illegible] when I [illegible] a sword [illegible]

d If at any time

e War, or any sore judgment.

f Choose out a man, who lives on the Borders, knows the Avenues, and the wayes, the Enemy will most likely come to assault them.

g Appoint him to watch the Coasts, that they may not be surprised.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:3
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
h Of the Enemy, or any other danger, which he may foresee, in any of the causes, or forerunners of it.

i i. e. Coming, approaching to the Land.

k Sound the alarm, the sound of the Trumpet is a warning, yet to this sometimes 'tis necessary to add a warning by word of mouth, and tell people, brought together by the Trumpet, what he seeth.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:4
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Heb. He that hearing heareth.

m Considers not, and minds not what he hears, who hears, and do's not consider, he turns a deaf ear to the meaning, tho' not to the sound of the Trumpet.

n Apprehends not, nor will be made apprehensive of the danger, to provide for resisting, or flying the sword.

o Destroy him.

p The guilt and blame of his blood, of his death.

q Shall never be charged on any, but himself.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:5
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
r He heard, as well as others who escap't, and he might have delivered himself, as they did, who took warning.

s He is the only cause of his own death.

t Shall save his life.

u Himself, preserve his own person.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:6
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
x Neglect his charge, which is to give the Alarm.

y But, unwarned, are surprized by the Enemy.

z Punisht by the Lord for his sins, and trespasses formerly done, and he is destroyed under the present fault of not watching, which is a fault in every one, that is so secure in time of War.

a The guilt of that blood.

b Charge upon, and for it punish the Watchman, who sinn'd in not giving warning.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:7
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: chap. 3.17, &c.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:9
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: These three verses are the same with the 17th, 18th, 19th verses of the third chap. where see them explained.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:10
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
c Declare to them from me.

d The residue of the Two Tribes, which are brought to Babylon, or else to those already there, and hear their Brethren are on the way thitherward, since Ierusalem was taken.

e Thus ye discourse among your selves, object against God, and his Prophet, and your own Duty, some of you out of infirmity, others out of perverseness.

f The unpardoned guilt, and the unsupportable punishment of our sins, who were warned, and took not warning, do thus, as in the wasting our Countrey, burning our City, abolishing the publick Worship of God, come upon us, we shall pine away, consume, 'tis too late to hope, 'twill be better with us now, we should have heard, and followed the Counsel earlier, if we would have delivered our own souls: if the Prophet spake true at first, there is no hope, say the weaker, if there be hope now after so peremptory Menaces, and so great Execution, the Prophet did not speak truth say the perverse, and so concluded they would, as they were, run the hazard.

chap. 24.23.

g How can it be better with us, if the threats be true, and sure, 'twill be worse, if not true, how are his promises to be rested on, that 'twill be better.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:11
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
h Vid. chap. 5. ver. 11. and chap. 16. ver. 48. let. f, and 17. chap. 16. let. g.

h See chap. 18. ver. 23. and v[illegible]r. 32. l[illegible]t. a.

2 Sam. 14.14. chap. 18.23, 32.

k Here an ellipsis, but I have pleasure in the seasonable return, the Sinner makes from Sin to Holiness, and from Death to L[illegible]fe.

l O leave sin, cease to do evil, be perswaded to repent, it will please me to pardon your faults, and to throw away the r[illegible]d, and to save your persons.

chap. 13 [illegible]1.

m Death is your choice, not mine, so long as you go on in the way that is not Good; who[illegible]o sinneth against me, wrongeth his own soul, and love to [illegible]n is interpretatively a love, and choosing of Death. 'Tis your culpable will, not my severe resolution, that you die.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:12
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
chap. 3.20[illegible] and 1[illegible].24.

n See chap. 3. ver. 20. and chap. 18. ver. 24. tot.

o Vid. chap. 18. ver. 21, 22. tot.

p See chap. 3. ver. 20. and 18. chap 24. where the same things are explained.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:13
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
q Who hath in his life, for what is past, kept the Law, and forborn evil, hath done what is right and good, and not done what is evil, both which parts of this Righteousness are described in chap. 18. ver. 5, 6, 7, 8, 9.

r Make him promise of doing him good, and giving him Life, Peace, every Blessing, and Happiness.

s If he conclude former Righteousness is sufficient, and therefore turn to ways of sin pleasing to an evil heart.

t Give himself to doing evil, as 'twere his work.

u No regard shall be had to what he had done, he doth himself practically renounce it, and interpretatively recant his doing it.

x In his Apostacy, and backs[illegible]idden state.

y Shall be punished, his comforts shall be taken away, or die in his hand, he shall live, and die miserably.

z His iniquity, and punishment of it, and this is emphatically repeated, as chap. 18.26.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:14
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
a Chap. 18. ver. 21. let. f.

Heb. judgment and justice.

b Ibid.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:15
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
c Chap. 18. ver. 7. let. q.

Exod. 22.1, 4. Lev. 6.2, 4. Num. 5.6, 7.

d Ibid. let. r.

e 'Tis not a sinless life here required, or supposed, but a Life in which a man doth not habitually, and wilfully work iniquity.

f Vid. chap 18. ver. 9. let. i.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:16
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
g See chap. 18. ver. 16. tot.

As the threat against a Righteous man that proves a presumptuous Apostate, was stated in the former part of the 12th, and in the whole 13th verse, so in these three verses the case of a Repenting and Reforming sinner is stated, and determined to his encouragement, and comfort, and they are the same with chap. 18. ver. 21, 22, and with ver. 27, 28. which see.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:17
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
ver. 20

These Impious, obstinate quarrelers will accuse, and do condemn the just, and Holy God, that they may acquit themselves, see this verse explained, chap. 18. ver. 25, 29.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:19
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: In these two verses the cases are so clearly stated, that 'tis as clear as the Sun, the wayes of God are very just, and that none but ignorant Atheists, would think or surmise otherwise.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:20
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
chap. 18.25. verse 17.

h Call you to account plead with you, and pass sentence.

i This is added, to rouse every one up to repent of all sins, and of this particularly.

k A terrible threat, and I know not how a greater could be denounced against sinners then this, God infinitely Holy, and perfectly just, will judge them according to their unequal, unrighteous, sinful wayes, and according to his inflexible justice. And if God enter thus into judgment, who can stand in sight?

Still blinded prejudice quarrels.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:21
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
chap. 1.2.

l That is one year, and five months after the thing was done, and Temple burnt, and the City sacked.

m One whose own care, but Gods wonderful Providence had much more befriended him, perhaps it might be one of those, that yeilded to the Babylonians before, but was resolved to see the upshot of all.

n Likely giving a particular account of the whole.

o Ierusalem.

2 King. 25.

p Taken and plundered the inhabitants, or slain, or Captives, and the City sackt razed, and burnt.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:22
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
q The powerful influence of the Prophetick spirit, inspired me, and prepared me for what followed.

r Not that the prophet was dumb through impotence, and inability to speak, for he had prophesied against many Nations, but he was forbidden to say any thing of the Jews, to threaten, warn, counsel, or command, chap. 24.25 26, 27. and chap. 29.21. but now the spirit moved me to speak, and continued his motion, till the messenger came, and ever after, for God did not command him silence any more.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:24
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
s Who were left behind, having either hid themselves but now come out of their holes, or returned from neighbour Countreys, whither they fled or permitted by the Conqueror to stay and plant Vineyards.

t Places once very fruitful and abounding with people, but now by the spoil of the Souldiers, emptied of inhabitants, and made as a desolate Wilderness.

x Our Father had hereditary right to all this land, when but one, and he multiplyed to a great Company, and so they possessed the Land, we Children of Abraham, though diminisht, are many, and the Divine goodness will surely appear then, and continue to us both right, and possession, and we shall fill the Land, and recover our former state and priviledges

y 'Twas given by promise to us the Seed, as well as to our Progenitour, nay more 'tis given us in possession, we dwell in it, when Abraham had not one foot of it in his possession.

z The perpetual inheritance is ours. Thus with vain fallacious arguments they cheat one another.

u Thus think and speak, thus with vain reasonings they deceive themselves.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:25
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
a Remove them from this dangerous carnal confidence, and shew them what they do, by that, what they are, how far from Abrahams seed, his genuine Seed.

Lev. 3.17. and 7.26. and 17.10. Deut. 12.16.

b What ever might be the reason why, tis most certain, this was forbidden, Gen. 9.4. Lev. 17.14. and 19.26. they sinned by violating this Law.

c Honouring, praying, depending on, and committing your selves to the protection, and guidance of those dumb Idols. Vid. c. 18.6. let. k.

d Innocent blood, ye are murtherers.

e Polluted with such, and many other heinous sins, and what colour of hope can you have, that you shall possesse the Land? The question includes a peremptory denial.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:26
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
f You trust to your Sword, and stand with it as 'twere drawn ready to kill and slay, you do all with violence, and force, not regarding what is right and equal and fear no restraints or punishments.

g Idolatry, or other wickedness not to be named.

h Adultery is so common among you, that 'tis no bold hyperbole to say, every one defiles his neighbours wife.

i And can such sinners flatter themselves, that they shall inherit the Land promised to a holy and good Father, and to the like Seed? Will not the Land spew Jewish sinners out, as it did spew out such Canaanit[illegible]h sinners?

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:27
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
k The ruinous heaps of Cities, or Towns, in which some sorry habitations might possibly be found by them.

l The Chaldean Souldier ransacking all places, and either expecting, or by chance finding them there, shall kill in revenge of G[illegible]da[illegible]iahs death, and I[illegible]mael, with others shall destroy some of them.

m That wanders in the Fields shall be a prey to Lions, or other ravenous Beasts, that will multiply in that ruined Countrey.

chap. 3[illegible].

Heb. [illegible] him.

n Out of the reach of Men, and Beasts, my hand shall reach, I will send the Pestilence, that shall sweep them away.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:28
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
o I do purpose to destroy utterly all in this Land, and what can escape, when salvage Beasts, cruel men, and a pestilential Air all concur to ruine the Land?

Heb. [illegible] on and [illegible].

chap. [illegible]. and 24.21. and 30.6[illegible].

p The stately, and pompous shews of her strength, and her former riches and power.

q On which were Vineyards and Oliveyards, where the joyful sounds of the Vintage, and Harvests did glad the heart, there shall be utter desolation.

r No man daring to venture for fear of wild Beasts, or Pestilential Air, or Famine in those wasted Mountains.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:29
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: I would have had them acknowledged me to be the Lord by my blessings, which beautifyed the Land, by my holy precepts, which directed to piety, and justice, by my Mercy and kindness towards them, but they despised my mercy, broke my law, abused my bounty, and now by the punishment of their sins, as I threatned, and by laying the Land most waste, they shall be constrained to own, and submit to me, as the Lord.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:30
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
s Captives in Babylon.

t Thy, not my people, God doth debase, degrade, and disown them.

u As men now do in Cities or Towns, so then they stood up to the Wall, when meeting in the Streets, they would talk together.

x Others got into the porches or doors of their houses, this they did to tell each other what news of their Countrey.

z Come I pray let us go up to the Prophet, the true Prophet, and enquire what God hath revealed to him, and what he may reveal unto us, whether any, or when will that end of our sorrows be.

y And all ends in this at last.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:31
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
chap. 14.1[illegible] and 20.1 &c.

Heb. [illegible] ing to the [illegible] ing of the [illegible]

a Flocking to the School of some famous Doctor, or as Men and Women flock to hear some famous Preacher, or as they were wont to the Synagogues to hear their learned Scribes.

Or, my [illegible] sit before thee.

b So we find the Elders of Iudah, chap. 8.1. which see at let. f. so the Disciples of the great Rabbies sat at their feet, so is Saul said to be brought up at the feet of Gamal[illegible]el.

c By their outward deportments, you might judge them to be my people, and hear seemingly very attentive.

d They do onely hear what thou sayest, but they will not do it.

Isa. 29.12.

e All their love is but from teeth outward, either to me, my word, or my Prophet, saith God,

Heb. [illegible] loves, [illegible].

f Their desire, love and care is about their gain, how to make thriving bargains, how to place out and secure their money with excessive, and intolerable usury and increase.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:32
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Heb. song of loves.

These Iews esteem, and regard thee, and what thou sayest, as men regard a skilful Musician, who to a well tuned instrument hath sung the praises of vertue, or of vertuous men; it pleaseth their ear, but it doth not frame their hearts and life to vertue. They loved him for his eloquent lamentation, and reproof of their Enemies, and for foretelling that they should fall, and saying nothing against them, and their sins for these three years past, but when he exhort, or disswades them to duty, or from sin, they'l hear, not do.

entries.title: Ezekiel 33:33
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
chap. 2.5.

When all thou hast prophesied against the Iews shall, as that thou prophesiedst against the Nations, come to pass to their ruin, they shall know thou wast no Musician but a Prophet sent of God, to forewarn you to fly from wrath, not imployed by Men, to please their wanton ear and fancy.

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:2
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Jer. 23.1, 11.

a The rulers of the people, both Political, as Kings, Magistrates, and Princes, as also Ecclesiastical, Priests, and Prophets.

b The two Tribes and the few, that out of the ten did adhere to the house of David.

c The command is repeated to encourage, and engage the Prophet to his work.

d Ezekiel speaks, but these Rulers must know 'tis God that speaks by him.

e They have been principal causes of many sins, and exemplary actors in other sins, for which many woes were threatned, many already are come and the rest will come, in which woes these Rulers shall have more then ordinary share.

f Contrive their own ease, advantage, honour, and ambitious projects.

g Let the consciences of these Rulers Ecclesiastical and Political speak, ought they not as Shepherds take care of the Sheep committed to their care?

h The Sheep, both whole Flocks and the single Sheep, whole societies, and particular members of them.

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:3
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Zech. 11.16.

i Rather the milk which insatiably, and without measure you devour: you exhaust their purses, and weaken their Estates by Tributes, exacted by extortions, so the Temporal Rulers, and the Spiritual Rulers had their methods, and arts to milk them dry, these lived on the sins of the people.

k With best and finest, as best suiting with your pride, and luxury, on which you force the people to bestow so much, they have not to clothe themselves and theirs, this was mighty oppression.

l Contrive methods for a seeming legal course to forfeit, first the Life, and next the Estate of the well fed, the rich and wealthy and then make merry and Feast, as voluptuous unfaithful shepherds feast on the fattest of the Sheep in their masters sold.

m Take no care to lead, protect, provide for, and watch over them, but as idle shepheards, feasted with the fattest, let the rest starve for any thing they care.

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:4
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
n The weak and languishing, such there are in the Church, and State.

o With your hand, countenance and counsel, so these Metaphorical shepheards should as the other strengthen their sheep, with carrying them into good and quiet pastures.

p The sheep in our Pastures are subject to many sicknesses, the sheep in Church and State to more, and Shepheards in both should be as Physicians to heal them, but here these did not so.

q Sometime violent and ravenous beasts break their bones, sometimes the stronger and fatter sheep bruise or break them, these should the shepheards bind up, violent oppressours in the State, and such in Church broke many then, but these shepheards bound them not up.

s Sheep wander, and lose themselves, shepheards should seek such and bring them home, many political sheep among the Jews wandered from their Countrey, their King, Religion and God, and these careless Rulers never sought them.

1 Pet. 9.3.

t With hard hand that held fast all, that should look like royal power and priviledge, and rigorously executed all their grievous Laws, and Edicts.

u Such as the Egyptians used toward the Jews, Exod. 1.13, 14. instead of acting like shepheards, these Tyrants in the Jewish Polity, acted like merciless butchers in Church and State.

r Sheep are often driven out of the pasture, frighted, hunted, and pursued by Dogs, or other mischievous Creatures, these the Shepheard should find our, and bring back in Church and State, there were many such frighted and driven by fierce men like Dogs running upon them, but the Jewish Rulers took no care to enquire for them, or to bring them back to their own Countrey.

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:5
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
x My neglected Sheep.

y By the inroads, and invasions of their Enemies, that broke in like devouring Beasts.

Or, without a shepherd, so v. 8.

z No vigilant, faithful good shepherd that loved the Flock, and of love studied its welfare.

a Were made a prey of, and devoured by Syrians, Ammonites, Moabites, Edomites, &c. all their Neighbours might then devour them.

b Signifie men, troops of Robbers, and spoilers.

c As sheep scattered are easily devoured by every hungry Wolf or Fox.

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:6
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
c These shepherds forgot, the flock was not their propriety, but God will not lose his propriety in them, nor shall shepherds find at last they were more then Gods stewards and accountable.

d When endangered, afrighted, pursued they got upon the Mountains by their own choice, or carried away by Enemies, or it may refer to their wandring after Idols Worshipped in High places, or perhaps to Kingdoms and States and great Cities, compared to Mountains, that there they might find what they could not at home, quiet and safety.

e The same thing in like words.

f They were if any among the Jews could be called so, my flock, that were so used, not the Swine, and Goats and unclean Beasts, that by whole Herds rested undisturbed, 'twas Bar[illegible]ch and Ieremiah were fain to hide.

g They were dispersed through male-administration to all parts of the known World; 'tis an Hyperbole that speaks a mighty scattering.

h The shepherds were contented nay glad they were rid of them, neither principal Officers searcht, nor inferior sought after them.

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:7
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: i The Rulers, King of Israel, Princes, High Priest and Priests and pretended Prophets, hear ye; God speaks in the stile and manner of one greatly incensed.

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:8
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
k See ver. 5. let. a. b.

l Ibid. let. z

m Government and Governours are by Gods appointment, and here he owns the careless, worst of Rulers as his shepherds.

n Verse 6. let. h.

o Verse 2. let. f.

p Vid. ver. 3. let. p.

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:9
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: Vid. verse 7. tot.

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:10
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
q They have provokt me to displeasure to be their Enemy, and I will appear, and act so, they are Enemies to my sheep, yet pretended to be shepherds, I will be an open Enemy to them.

r To Zedekiah his Princes, the Priests, and Prophets, all the ruling part in Ierusalem.

s I will require both account first, and next by severe punishing, as Zedekiah his Children, &c. found.

t Turn them out of my service, that honourable employment, so was the King and Princes of Iudah turned out of all by the King of Babylon by whom God made good this his word.

u Their profit ceased with the ceasing of their Authority, and they could no more milk, fleece or slay the flock, when 'twas taken out of their hand.

x They should have delivered them out of the hands of violence, since they did not I will deliver, save and rescue this flock which is mine.

y This speaks that these Shepherds had been Lions or Bears, or Wolves more then Shepherds, and therefore out of their mouths not hands God will deliver.

z So the flock shall no more be devoured by them.

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:11
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
a The construction is emphatical in the Heb. and well exprest here, I the owner, the lover, the maker, the great shepherd, even I, who committed them to your care, never submitted them to your rapine and cruelty, who am as angry with you for devouring them, as I am zealous for their welfare

b Will demand them of you, I know how many I delivered to your keeping, and I expect an account of so many again, I will see in what state, and condition they are too.

c Vide ver. 5. let. s. and ver. 6. let. h. under your hand many are, but under my hand, not one shall be lost.

entries.title: Ezekiel 34:12
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Heb. according to the seeking.

d He doth gently gather them together, counteth them, brings them to the fold, views what they have suffered, whether lame or torn and binds up, and healeth; if any are wanting, he looks till he findeth them, and does bring them back, so will I, saith the Lord, if the shepherd find the Wolf, or Lion among them or near them, he will either kill or drive him away, so will God if under-servants have been careless, they shall be warned or turned away, So here, &c,
